title: How an Absurd Tragedy Happened: "There Was No Event on the Bund This Year"
excerpt: The government has done all it can to contain the damage from the Bund disaster, but its own inadequate response is what set the disaster in motion.
body:
The government has done all it can to contain the damage from the Bund disaster, but its own inadequate response is what set the disaster in motion.

On its face the affair is absurd: government departments assumed the public already knew the light show had moved, and built every part of their preparations on that assumption.

That absurdity grew out of another bad decision. A closely watched event, perhaps the biggest public New Year's Eve celebration Shanghai had held in recent years, was quietly moved to a place far fewer people knew about.

The result: this popular event lost roughly 300,000 on-site spectators that New Year's Eve, and 36 innocent people lost their lives.





On the second day of the new year, at Bund Origin (Waitanyuan) in Shanghai, several workers were taking apart the light show's steel-frame main stage and viewing stands. The purple curtains on two large display frames had not yet come down, and still bore the words "2015 New Year's Eve Light Show." An event that usually draws more than 200,000 spectators had this year drawn only a few hundred, and ended in near silence. With the tragedy 500 meters away, it looked all the more dim and out of place.

A few days after the disaster, the area beside the statue of Chen Yi in the middle of the square was turned into a memorial, fenced off with black iron railings. A steady stream of people came to mourn those who died during the New Year's Eve light show, and a dozen or so police officers formed a human wall to keep apart two streams of people moving in opposite directions. A few female students who had come together broke down in tears in the square. On the other side of the flower-laying area, a victim's family had brought a Taoist priest to perform a ritual.

A hundred meters straight ahead of the Chen Yi statue, a flight of steps leads up to the Bund viewing platform. The steps come in two flights, the first of 8 steps and the second of 9, with a landing about 1.5 meters wide between them. Climb these 17 steps and you reach the viewing platform, three or four meters above the square. The 36 visitors never made it up. At a light show that had gone through one upheaval after another, they died in panic and crush.

![Mourners at the memorial area beside the Chen Yi statue on the Bund](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160605215846L0TOiVhURjSQnKYr.jpg-w600)



I

Every city lays on something impressive to welcome the new year. After several New Year's Eve celebrations at Xintiandi's Taiping Lake, Times Square on Huaihai Road, Century Square on East Nanjing Road and elsewhere, Shanghai began planning a new kind of New Year's Eve party in 2011.

Its centerpiece was the light show people later talked about so much. That year the organizers picked 3D projection technology that had been used at major international events abroad. The projection area was a stretch of the Bund's "international architecture complex," from the Pudong Development Bank Building to the Customs House clock tower, 108 meters wide and 76 meters high. Residents and tourists on the Bund, in Pudong, and even out on the river could all see it.

![The light show projected onto the historic buildings along the Bund](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160605215847AQ5LGI2rs0z4cgNk.jpg-w600)

Sun Zhongming, head of the Huangpu District tourism bureau, [told Jiefang Daily](http://www.jfdaily.com/jfzy/201401/t20140103_20503.html) that the show was finally sited between the Pudong Development Bank Building and the Customs House clock tower because the bank building had once been "the most luxurious building from the Suez Canal to the Bering Strait," while the clock tower suited the countdown theme. "It freezes history and tells the present at the same time. There is no more fitting place."

The party, prepared in only about two months, ended up with three hosts, the Huangpu District People's Government, the Shanghai Municipal Tourism Administration and Shanghai Media Group (SMG), and two organizers, the Huangpu District tourism bureau and Dragon TV. On the operational side, the light show was handled by SMG's large-events department and by Shanghai Huanwei Digital Creative Technology Co., Ltd. (Huanwei Digital), an SMG subsidiary. After checking business registration records, QDaily confirmed that Huanwei Digital's legal representative, Wang Jianqiang, was formerly deputy director of Shanghai Radio and Television and a vice president of SMG, and is now [chief technology officer of the merged Shanghai Media Group](http://www.chinatimes.cc:8200/hxsb/news/gongsi/140919/1409192329-137691.html).

Xu Sheng (a pseudonym used at his request), a Huanwei Digital employee who has helped prepare the Bund light show for several years, told QDaily that for a production company like theirs, the normal process is to start planning the year's script with the show's directors and the relevant government departments three to four months ahead. Once the theme is set, they spend about two more months producing, testing and rehearsing the visual side of the show.

![Projection equipment and crew preparing the light show](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201606052158482IzaPBGrj8VEu46o.jpg-w600)

According to [another Jiefang Daily report](http://stock.hexun.com/2015-01-01/171977070.html), the theme of the first light show in 2011 was settled in a rush on December 28, by Huangpu District head Zhou Wei himself. Luckily, with 52 ultra-high-definition projectors in 8 sets from the projector maker Christie, plus 3D modeling, that year's show was a hit. Over the next three years, with outside help from [the Olympics lighting design team](http://adv.smg.cn/page/2011-12-09/876.html) and [the art direction team behind *The Fifth Element*](http://ent.sina.com.cn/v/m/2012-11-23/12103794781.shtml), it kept making technical leaps. For the sake of the effect, the Shanghai Street Lighting Center even [designed a single-lamp control system](http://210.77.176.143/xwzx/gsyw/yxfc/12/300018.shtml) for the 60 street lamps inside the projection area.

The [*Shanghai Yearbook 2013*](http://www.shanghai.gov.cn/shanghai/node2314/node24651/n32098/n32146/u21ai866746.html) describes the Bund light show that welcomed New Year's Day 2014 like this:

"Last year's 3D light show was upgraded to 4D this year, merging the stage, the street and the building walls into a single space. Combining imagery, lasers, lighting and other technologies, and pairing projected displays, wire rigs and lasers with live performers, it took the audience through Shanghai's development since the port opened, in 9 minutes. Dragon TV broadcast it live worldwide in full, drawing relays from mainstream media such as the BBC, CNN and NHK and linking in real time with global cities such as New York, London, Paris, Tokyo and Sydney, making it a New Year countdown event with global influence."

According to the yearbook, the show drew more than 200,000 spectators on site, and total foot traffic in the Bund area that day came close to 300,000.

II

Crowds that size raised safety worries. The 300,000 visits recorded on the day of the light show for New Year 2014 were already the most the Bund could hold, and almost the entire Bund viewing area was overloaded that day.

[According to Southern Weekend](http://www.infzm.com/content/106937), several sources at Bund Origin, in the Huangpu police and on the light show's directing team all said that using Bund Origin's natural space limits to ease the security burden may have been one reason for this year's move.

[What Caixin learned](http://china.caixin.com/2015-01-03/100770396.html) was that as early as the application stage in early November 2014, the major events office of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau had already rejected the Bund light show, because the previous year's New Year's Eve show had drawn too many people, beyond capacity, and holding it again would be a safety risk.

![Crowds on the Bund at a previous New Year's Eve light show](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160605215848jagLpEt3oSqz46GM.jpg-w600)

Xu Sheng told QDaily that with just over a month to go, there was still no final answer on whether the event would go ahead, or where, or at what scale. That is plainly not how a large event normally moves forward.

Safety concerns led to a major safety disaster. That is where the whole affair's absurdity lies.

On December 25, 2014, Shanghai papers including [Xinmin Evening News](http://xmwb.xinmin.cn/html/2014-12/25/node_4.htm) and [Oriental Morning Post](http://epaper.dfdaily.com/dfzb/html/2014-12/25/node_7.htm) ran reports with photos announcing a New Year's Eve light show at Bund Origin.

How many people those newspaper reports actually told about the move is anyone's guess.

Many travel websites, in their December 2014 lists of Shanghai New Year's Eve attractions, still gave the light show's location as the Bund, not Bund Origin. "The Shanghai Bund 'light show' is a beautiful visual feast that has dazzled people on New Year's Eve two years running. Lights of every color play across the tall buildings, utterly brilliant. The 2015 'Bund light show' welcomes you!" read one on the Nanbeiyou website. Even the local city-life portal [Bendibao](http://sh.bendibao.com/tour/20141124/118511.shtm) did not note that the 2015 Bund New Year's Eve light show had moved to Bund Origin until December 31 itself.

Wu Wei came with his girlfriend from near Hongqiao Airport. A little after 10 p.m., he got off the subway at East Nanjing Road, the station nearest the Bund.

That surprised him a little. At the previous year's New Year's Eve event, the East Nanjing Road stations on Lines 2 and 10 had been closed from 7 p.m. This year they stayed open.

By the time he reached Chen Yi Square, the crowd had all but stopped moving. He and his girlfriend squeezed forward for more than half an hour and covered less than 10 meters toward the viewing platform. Worried by the crush, she held his hand tightly. "It's fine, it'll ease up in a bit." Wu Wei had no thought of the stampede to come: every year the place was packed, and every year nothing happened.

III

Wu Wei had reason to be calm. Shanghai has plenty of experience handling large events.

A Shanghai Tourism Administration [notice from more than a year earlier](http://lyw.sh.gov.cn/lyj_website/HTML/big5shlyj/lyj_ywzx_qxdt/2014-01-06/Detail_112924.htm) shows how thorough the preparations used to be. To make sure nothing went wrong, Huangpu police got involved three months before New Year's Day 2014, just as planning for the light show began, assessing risks and drawing up plans. For the Bund light show on New Year's Eve 2013, Shanghai police deployed 6,000 officers, 2,000 more than the year before. Officers from different departments worked together, large fire engines stood by, and many police cadets took part.

Beyond the police, the Shanghai work safety bureau and the municipal quality supervision bureau jointly inspected the safety of the show's moving equipment, and the municipal construction and transportation commission posted staff at the main shut-off valves and switches for the Bund's water, power and gas, ready to cut them the moment anything went wrong. On the Huangpu River, the maritime safety administration added patrol boats.

A grass-roots government employee also told QDaily that on light-show nights in earlier years, large numbers of police were deployed across the Bund to keep order. Besides police, community volunteers from the districts involved were also organized to help with security.

An employee of the Bund Scenic Area Management Office [told The Beijing News](http://news.sina.com.cn/c/2015-01-02/023931352578.shtml) that at previous Bund light shows, the police running on-site security set up four "lines of defense," radiating out from the Bund viewing platform at the center, and a command post adjusted the flow of people based on live video. Only a small number of pass holders could reach the core viewing platform; most spectators were held back on the outer side of Zhongshan East 1st Road. Those controls kept the scene manageable.

With security like that, no wonder Wu Wei was sure "it'll ease up in a bit." But for the light show before New Year's Day 2015, security had been scaled back.

On January 1, 2015, Cai Lixin, deputy commander of the command center of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau's Huangpu branch, told a news conference that the police had underestimated the crowd on the Bund on December 31 and had at first assigned only a little over 700 officers. A year earlier, at the New Year's Eve celebration that welcomed 2014, there had been more than 6,000, and Bai Shaokang, then Shanghai's vice mayor and head of the municipal public security bureau, had gone to the Bund in person to oversee security.

![Police at the scene on the Bund](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160605215849yvpQP1OS5HuLU2JK.jpg-w600)

Traffic controls were cut back even more sharply. Take the light show for New Year's Day 2014. [Public records show](http://gaj.sh.gov.cn/shga/gweb/xxnr_view.jsp?pa=58e282badd297ff317c00220e6c4da04cc90db2840dd943b2683b221256d4f314f9de1564b0228de71f9aeed6d911908100a0a027ea0dfc076c62d15790546136bbb7b062e834a3fa74e545e8611991ec0073cdb280a2c290ca4498a22f48bc59ad10ad11e5f4b213d05d4684a12816419783fac30e49608cb55297146ae858576c4d46f8054fd6a) that on December 23, 2013, the Shanghai Public Security Bureau issued a New Year's Eve traffic control notice under the Road Traffic Safety Law. It temporarily banned all vehicles from the area running from the junction of Zhongshan East 1st Road and Beijing East Road along Zhongshan East 1st Road (inclusive), Yan'an East Road, Middle Sichuan Road (inclusive) and Beijing East Road, back to the junction of Beijing East Road and Zhongshan East 1st Road. The East Nanjing Road stations on Lines 2 and 10 were closed. This year, traffic controls covered only Yuanmingyuan Road and South Suzhou Road in front of Bund Origin.

Cai Lixin said that because there was no event on the Bund this year, the relevant regulations meant that an open public area like the Bund could only be placed under control after a public notice had been issued in advance, unless an emergency occurred.

Zhang Jianli has run a stall near the Bund for 6 years. In his view, the Bund is a landmark with huge crowds all year round, and the lack of a light show there was no reason to cut security. He said he had not known about the light show at Bund Origin, and even if he had, he would not have pushed his cart over there. "Every New Year's Eve on the Bund, the crowds have never been small. Over there (at Bund Origin), even with an event, there won't be many people." Geography alone guarantees the crowds: the Bund is the best place to look across the river at Lujiazui, and both the Huangpu River sightseeing cruises and the Bund promenade are here.

Everything about that night, the tragedy and the absurdity, comes down to one thing: there was no event on the Bund this year.

IV

People still headed for the Bund. [Xinhua reported](http://www.sc.xinhuanet.com/content/2015-01/02/c_1113851685.htm) that by 8:30 p.m., the crowd on the Bund was already approaching the size of the previous year's light show welcoming 2014, far more than expected.

Meanwhile, the place where the light show was actually held fell far short of its expected audience.

[According to Caixin](http://china.caixin.com/2015-01-03/100770396.html), this year's show was led by the Huangpu District government rather than the Shanghai municipal government, and attendance was capped at 2,000. A security guard at the venue recalled to QDaily that about 500 people came to watch that day.

![The light show stage at Bund Origin](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160605215850pLbyP1HYlnXdiZ0q.jpg-w600)

QDaily reached a woman who had tried to sell a ticket for the Bund Origin show online.

The woman, who asked not to be named, said the ticket had been a gift from a friend and had no price printed on it. Busy with work, she had hoped to pass it on, but for several days nobody got in touch, and the ticket was marked "not transferable," so she gave up.

That fits what other guards at the venue said about tickets: there was no ticket office at the entrance to the main venue; every ticket was a free, unsellable ticket supplied by sponsors, and guards checked each one before letting people in. And because the entrance was some distance from the main stage, and the stage itself had shrunk by nearly three quarters, the sightlines were much reduced, which all but ruled out watching from farther away or from other angles nearby.

![The fenced-off venue at Bund Origin](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160605215850X3WpEiGIQ8kfK6or.jpg-w600)

For Wu Wei and the other visitors, the near-identical names of Bund Origin and the Bund, along with how closed off Bund Origin was, both physically and in what was said about it, made them all the more inclined to stick with what they knew: stay in Chen Yi Square, where they had always seen a grand show, and wait for the lights to begin.

QDaily asked five street vendors around the Bund. None of them knew the light show had moved either.

And when some people later did start heading for Bund Origin to see the real light show, they were no longer allowed through.

At 11:35 p.m., streams of people moving in opposite directions collided on the slope in Chen Yi Square on the Bund. Some fell in the crush, and the scene began to spin out of control.

At 11:40 p.m., those pinned underneath were weakening. By the time the crowd finally dispersed, a dozen or so people lay collapsed on the stairs.

At 11:50 p.m., more and more police arrived. It was already too late.
